sections.COMMENTS:
ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
The source region of the 1627 earthquake falls on the westward prolongation of the well-known Mattinata Fault System (and its offshore continuation in the Gondola structural high), and about 12 km east of the 31 October, 2002 Molise seismogenic source. We suggest, according to Valensise et al. (2004), that the 2002 Molise earthquakes may explain the poorly understood 1627 earthquake. In the 2002, 31 October-1 November, two M 5.8 right-lateral strike-slip earthquakes occurred. They were caused by rupture on an E-W subvertical rupture plane. The 2002 Molise earthquakes struck areas characterized by low seismic release east of the Apennines axis and were generated by previously undetected relatively deep E-W faults.
We believe that these two earthquakes shed light on the style of seismogenic faulting of the whole region. The aligned seismogenic sources of the 2002 Molise earthquakes, of the 1627 earthquake, and of the Mattinata Fault System are E-W dextral strike-slip faults, in agreement with present-day stress field orientations from borehole breakouts.
sections.OPEN QUESTIONS:
1) Is the E-W strike-slip fault system active as a whole, from Molise to the Adriatic Sea? Or is only a portion of it active?
1a) If the whole fault system is active, is the area located between the 31 October, 2002 Molise seismogenic source and the 1627 source a seismic gap?
1b) If the whole fault system is active, is the offshore Gondola structure a seismic gap?
2) Can the seismogenic source of the 1627 earthquake generate submarine landslides and an landslide-induced tsunami, according to an observed first large sea withdrawal?
sections.SUMMARIES:
Di Bucci and Mazzoli (2003)
They suggest that foreland deformation is characterised by active NW-SE compression, resulting in the reactivation of pre-existing east-west oriented structures as dextral strike-slip faults.
Patacca and Scandone (2004)
They present a comparison between the macroseismic field of the 1627 Gargano earthquake and the pattern of the faults identified in the subsurface. At a first glance they observe that only two faults can be responsible for the 1627 earthquake: the high-angle strike-slip fault of the Chieuti High, and the Apricena Fault. They observe that the strike-slip fault limiting the Chieuti High, linked to the Mattinata Fault, is inactive, and consequently they consider the Apricena Fault responsible for the 1627 event. The Apricena Fault, striking WNW-ESE and dipping towards SSW, is a normal fault that extends in the subsurface for about 30 kilometres.
Valensise et al. (2004)
These authors suggest that the 2002 Molise east-west faults may explain several large yet poorly understood historical earthquakes located between the crest of the Apennines and the Adriatic coastline. The seismogenic sources of the 2002 events appear to connect the Mattinata fault, a major active tectonic feature running from the west side of the South Adriatic depression to the western Molise border through the Gargano promontory. The source region of the 1627 earthquake fall on this east-west trend, on the westward prolongation of Mattinata fault, and about 12 km east of the 31 October, 2002 Molise source. The authors suggest that the entire system is active, and the 1627 seismogenic source is a portion of this system.
